kits.familyName: Choosing information that fits the task
setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}, and you are looking up information to finish a task.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you need the right information to answer a request.
detail: It is the middle of the afternoon.
pressure: {coworker3} says it is not worth the trouble.
You are in a hurry to finish.

tiers.1: Information about the wrong product can cause harm if you act on it.
tiers.2: An answer for the wrong situation misleads the person who asked.
tiers.3: A source written for another audience can hide the answer.
tiers.4: Extra numbers can bury the point of a report.

fact: You found three safety tips online, but only one names the product your workplace uses.
issues.short: the safety tips for other products
issues.action: Use the tip that names your product, and check it against the product's label.
issues.brief: use the tip for your product and check the label
issues.reason: Tips for a different product may not apply, and acting on them could cause harm.
issues.lesson: Use information only if it fits the exact product or situation you have.

shortcut.text: Combine all three tips so nothing is missed.
shortcut.why: Tips for other products may not fit yours, and mixing them can create a hazard.

clear: You already matched the tip to your product and checked its label.
issues.done: the tip is already checked against the label

fact: A customer asks whether a part fits their model, and the page you found lists parts for similar models.
issues.short: the parts page for similar models
issues.action: Find the listing for the customer's exact model before you answer.
issues.brief: find the listing for the exact model
issues.reason: Similar models can differ in small ways that decide whether a part fits.
issues.lesson: Look for information about the exact item, not a similar one.

shortcut.text: Tell them it fits, since similar models usually share parts.
shortcut.brief: say it fits because the models are similar
shortcut.why: Small differences between models decide whether a part fits.

clear: You already found the listing for the customer's exact model.
issues.done: the exact listing is already found

fact: A new coworker asks how to clock in, and the only guide you found is written for payroll staff.
issues.short: the guide written for payroll staff
issues.action: Write or find simple clock-in steps for a new employee.
issues.reason: A guide for payroll staff is full of details a new coworker does not need and may bury the steps.
issues.lesson: Choose or write information that suits the person who will use it.

shortcut.text: Hand over the payroll guide, since it contains the answer somewhere.
shortcut.why: The answer is buried among details that do not apply to a new coworker.
shortcut.mis: Having the answer somewhere is enough.

clear: You already wrote simple clock-in steps for the new coworker.
issues.done: the clock-in steps are already written

fact: Your report on this month's sales needs only this month's numbers, but the file you found covers the whole year.
issues.action: Use only this month's numbers, and note where they came from.
issues.reason: Extra numbers can hide the point of a report and make it harder to read.
issues.lesson: Use the part of the information that fits the task and leave the rest out.

shortcut.text: Include the whole year, so the reader has more to look at.
shortcut.why: Extra numbers bury the point, and the reader has to find the part that matters.
shortcut.mis: More data always makes a better report.

proceed.text: Carry on with your regular work, since nothing here needs action.
proceed.why: Each of these situations involves information that has to fit the task before you use it.
proceed.lesson: Check that information fits the exact product, situation, reader and scope before using it.

generic.text: Ask {coworker2} what they usually do and copy that.
generic.why: A coworker's habit is not the written guide, and it may be out of date.
generic.mis: Common practice is the same as the rule.

generic.text: Wait until {lead|the} brings it up before you act.
generic.why: The guide applies to you now, and waiting leaves the problem in place.
generic.mis: Someone else will raise it if it matters.

overcaution.text: Refuse to answer until every possible source has been checked and compared.
overcaution.why: The task needs the fitting source, not every source. Waiting delays the answer.
overcaution.mis: A good answer needs every source.

setup: A customer asks a question that needs a short written answer.

steps.text: Read exactly what the customer asked
Find information about that exact item
Keep only the part that answers it
Send the answer to the customer

rel: You cannot look for the right information before you know the question.
Trim the information you actually found.
process.lesson: Know the question, find the exact information, trim it, then send it.

title: Notes on finding information
intro: You are reading a coworker's draft advice on picking information for a task.
prompt: Which line gives advice that does not fit the task?
doc.lesson: Information has to fit the exact product, situation and reader before it is useful.

lines.text: Check that a tip names the product you are using.
lines.fine: Prevents acting on advice for something else.

bad.text: Follow any tip that mentions a similar product.
bad.why: A tip for a similar product may not fit yours and could cause harm.

lines.text: Write steps that suit the person who will use them.

bad.text: Give new coworkers the full expert guide so nothing is left out.
bad.why: Details they do not need can hide the steps they do.

lines.text: Include only the numbers the report needs.

bad.text: Include every number you found so readers can decide what matters.
bad.why: The writer should choose what matters. Extra numbers hide the point.

lines.text: Look up the exact model before answering a customer.

review.notes: Everyday information choices only; no source rankings or claims about outside organizations. Tiers: wrong product, wrong model, wrong audience, wrong scope.
